summary: A periodic list of the standardization status of Internet protocols, from the Internet Official Protocol Standards series. It is historic. It was replaced by RFC 3600.

eli5.summary: This was a status report card for Internet rules, updated now and then. It is historic and has been replaced by RFC 3600.

subtitle: A snapshot of Internet protocol standards as of October 2002.

tldr.problem: The standardization status of Internet protocols changes over time as new technologies mature and old ones are superseded.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3300 provides an updated periodic snapshot of all standardized Internet protocols, organized by standardization stage and including Best Current Practice documents, as of October 24, 2002.
tldr.outcome: Like its predecessor, this version became historic when superseded by RFC 3600, showing the evolution of the Internet standards landscape.

today: RFC 3300 is Historic and has been superseded by RFC 3600. Like RFC 3000 before it, it serves as a historical snapshot of the Internet standards landscape from 2002.

sections.title: Overview of Internet Standards
sections.content:
RFC 3300 is a snapshot of the state of standardization of protocols used in the Internet as of October 24, 2002. It is designated STD 1 and provides a comprehensive listing of official protocol standards, Best Current Practice documents, and protocols at various stages of the standards process. Like RFC 3000, it is not a complete index of all RFCs, but focuses on documents that represent actual protocol standards or guidance.

The document is published by the RFC Editor for the IETF, IAB, and IESG in accordance with RFC 2026. It serves as an official snapshot that helps the Internet community understand the current state of protocol standardization.
sections.eli5: This lists all the Internet rules that were officially approved or being worked on as of October 2002. It's similar to its predecessor but shows changes and progress over the past year.

sections.title: Standardization Categories
sections.content:
RFC 3300 organizes protocols into the same standardization categories used in RFC 3000. Standard protocols have completed the IETF standardization process and are ready for deployment. Draft Standard protocols are mature and nearly ready for standardization. Proposed Standard protocols are early in the standardization process and may change. Experimental protocols are not recommended for production use. Historic protocols are no longer recommended, typically because they have been obsoleted by better alternatives.

Best Current Practice documents provide recommendations and guidance for implementing standards and managing Internet operations, though they are not protocol specifications themselves.
sections.eli5: Protocols are organized by their maturity level: fully approved standards, nearly approved protocols, early proposals, experimental tests, and old outdated protocols that are no longer recommended.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 3000
sections.content:
Between RFC 3000 (October 2001) and RFC 3300 (October 2002), the Internet standards landscape evolved. New protocols moved up through the standardization levels, some protocols reached Standard status, and others were marked Historic. The document uses asterisks to mark protocols that are new or have changed status since the previous edition.

The document demonstrates the continuous process of Internet standardization, showing how the community works to evolve and improve the protocols that support the Internet.
sections.eli5: Over the year since the last report, some new Internet rules were approved, some old ones were replaced, and some were still being discussed. The asterisks show what changed.

sections.title: Key Standards Listed
sections.content:
RFC 3300 includes listings of fundamental Internet standards such as IP (RFC 791), TCP (RFC 793), UDP (RFC 768), DNS (RFC 1034-1035), SMTP (RFC 821), and FTP (RFC 959). As IPv6 and related technologies matured, they appear in this edition with new standards status. The document also shows emerging technologies in the Proposed Standard section, representing work on new protocols that would shape the Internet in coming years.

Historic protocols are documented, showing which older mechanisms have been replaced by modern alternatives, helping implementers understand which protocols to avoid.
sections.eli5: The list shows both the classic Internet protocols that make everything work and the newest protocols under development. It also shows which old protocols have been retired.

sections.title: Accessing Current Standards Information
sections.content:
While RFC 3300 provides a snapshot from October 2002, the RFC Editor maintains a continuously updated official standards list online that is refreshed daily. Developers and network administrators can access this current information from the RFC Editor web site (rfc-editor.org), retrieve documents via FTP, use the web-based search and retrieval system, or request documents via email.

The document explains these access methods and provides contact information for Internet organizations like the IETF, IAB, IRTF, and IANA, allowing readers to find authoritative information about any protocol.
sections.eli5: The document explains how to find the official list of approved Internet rules on the web or through email, and how to contact the organizations that manage Internet standards.
